senses.gloss:
rākṣasa-vivāha
(‘demoniac मर्रिअगे’)
------------------------------------------
Vivāha or मर्रिअगे has been listed by the smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस् as one of the sixteen सṁस्कारस् or sacraments.
Most of these works narrate eight forms of मर्रिअगे, of which the rākṣasavivāha is also one. It is actually equivalent to forcible abduction and rape in its crudest form and is a punishable offence in civilised societies. It is not even fit to be called विवाह or मर्रिअगे in the strictest sense of the term. It was included in the list only because it existed in certain primitive and barbarous societies. Perhaps it represented a kind of war-booty.
In course of time, as people settled down in towns and villages, building a civilised society, this form of मर्रिअगे became a symbolical one, especially among the kṣattriyas (warrior class) and very often, with the consent of the girl.
The classic examples found in the epics and the पुराणस् are those of कृष्ण and अर्जुन marrying रुक्मिणी and सुभद्रा.
Even in the case of the rākṣasa types, मर्रिअगे rites like the सप्तपदी were insisted upon to regularise the same.
See also VIVĀHA.

Rakṣoghna-mantras
(‘mantras that destroy evil spirits’)
------------------------------------------
Belief in the evil spirits and their capacity for harassing or even harming the good, is as old as the Ṛgveda itself. Prayers addressed to deities like अग्नि or इन्द्र and सोम, to ward off such evil spirits, are found in quite a few places in the Ṛgveda (4.4.1-15; 7.104.1-25; 10.87.1-25; 10.118.1-9; 10.162.1-6).These hymns, known as रक्षोघ्न-मन्त्रस्, are chanted at the appropriate places in sacrifices, while consecrating a newly-built होउसे, to prevent abortion in a woman who has conceived and so on.
The first group of 15 mantras is all addressed to अग्नि as Rakṣohā (destroyer of demons). He is compared to a king going on invasion for conquest, and requested to destroy the राक्षसस् or demons.
The second group of 25 mantras is addressed to इन्द्र and सोम, as also अग्नि and Maruts. Here also the prayers are addressed for the total annihilation of राक्षसस् and असुरस् (demons) by pushing them into the nether worlds from where there is no return.
The third group of 25 mantras is addressed to Agnī Rakṣohā with a request to burn up all the evil spirits who are trying to disturb the Vedic sacrifice.
The fourth group of 9 mantras also is addressed to Agnī Rakṣohā and praises him. He is then requested to destroy the female fiends called Yātudhānīs.
The last group of 6 mantras contains a special prayer indirectly addressed to अग्नि, to destroy all the diseases in a pregnant woman so that abortion or miscarriage is prevented.

Raktacāmuṇḍā
(‘[the destroyer] of the demons Caṇḍa and मुण्ड [who is] blood-red [in colour]’)
------------------------------------------
There are several aspects of the Divine मोथेर् (Śakti or पार्वती) of which रक्तचामुण्डा is also one. The Caṇḍī or Durgāsaptaśatī states that मोथेर् दुर्गा gave the name चामुण्डा to Kālī, who destroyed the two demons Caṇḍa and मुण्ड.
Raktacāmuṇḍā is sometimes known as योगेश्वरी also.
In her formless aspect, she is the power pervading the whole world.
Her form is described thus: She is red in colour, wears yellow garments as also bejewelled ornaments and a garland of severed human heads. The crescent मोओन् adorns her crest.
In her four hands she holds a sugarcane bow, arrow, discus and a lotus.
She is invoked for destroying one’s enemies.
See also CĀMUṆḌĀ.

Rākā
(‘the deity of the full-मोओन् day’)
------------------------------------------
Aṅgiras is one of the Prajāpatis, मिन्द्-born sons of ब्रह्मा, the creator. He married स्मृति and begot four daughters: अनुमति, राका, कुहू and सिनीवाली.
Rākā is the मोओन्-goddess, associated with the full-मोओन्. She is of considerable antiquity, being mentioned even in the Ṛgveda (2.32.4).
Along with सिनीवाली, she is worshipped in temples during the ceremonies of installation and consecration.
Rākā is invoked in mud-pots with fissures (chidra kumbha).
She is described as white in complexion with golden tinges. She wears red-garments and has two arms holding flowers. The हṁस or swan is her mount and banner. She is associated with the मुसिच् of lute and flute.
See also ANUMATI, KUHŪ and SINĪVĀLĪ.

rākṣasas
(‘beings from whom one seeks to protect oneself,’ ‘demons’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् and the epics mention various kinds of living beings in च्रेअतिओन्, of which the राक्षसस् are also one type.
The words असुरस् (antigods), दैत्यस् (sons of दिति, a wife of the sage कश्यप) and दानवस् (sons of Danu, another wife of कश्यप) are also often applied to them.
Though the general belief is that the राक्षसस् are extremely evil, wicked or malevolent spirits, they represent more a race or species of beings which can be broadly divided into three groups:
The yātudhānas and yakṣas who are by nature good, benevolent and skilful. They are semidivine and possess magical powers.
The titans, who are huge in size and mighty in strength. They are evil by nature. It is to kill them that the major gods like विष्णु, शिव or देवी appear in various forms.
The naktañcaras (demons and fiends) who wander about during nights, devouring human beings; and disturbing the penances of अस्चेतिच्स् as also the sacrifices of the sages.
The राक्षसस् are generally described as ugly, misshaped and with terrible tusks. They wear blue garments, live upon human flesh and become very powerful during nights.
They live below the solar regions.
In इचोनोग्रफ्य्, their images are shown in twelve tālas (See MŪRTIŚILPA-ŚĀSTRA for details.) or nine tālas.
Though eternally at loggerheads, the देवस् (gods) and the दानवस् or राक्षसस् (demons) were cousins, born of the same ड़थेर्, the sage कश्यप. Quite a few among the दानवस् distinguished themselves as great devotees of विष्णु or शिव. A few are: प्रह्लाद, विरोचन, बलि, Vṛtra, बाण and Śambara.
See also ASURAS, DAITYAS and DĀNAVAS.

Rakṣābandhana
(‘tying the amulet of protection’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् describe how इन्द्र, the king of the gods, who had been languishing after a particularly humiliating defeat at the hands of असुरस् or demons, was able to regain his sovereignty due to the power of the amulet tied on his hand by his queen Śacīdevī after some austerities. This is the origin of the रक्षाबन्धन festival. The rakṣās or rākhīs, prepared out of golden or yellow threads, with amulets, are first worshipped and then tied on the right hand. This tying may be done by priests who should be offered some money as दक्षिणा (fees) or by one’s sisters or even by sisterly ladies. The brothers should offer them some presents on the occasion. The famous मन्त्र uttered on this occasion seeks protection from it:
yena baddho balī राजा dānavendro mahābalaḥ । tena tvām abhibadhnāmi rakṣe mā cala mā cala ॥
(‘I tie on you that whereby Balī, the very powerful king of demons, was bound. O protective amulet! Don’t slip off, Don’t slip off!’)
On this day people of all religions, on the west coast, are in the habit of offering flowers and coconuts to the sea. It is a prayer and a request to make the sea voyage for merchant-vessels, safe and smooth.
